a MECE structure for 'where': version and device, term, grade/score, region and officer, acquisition source, new vs repeat
separates mix from rate
looks for an event: scorecard change, payment outage, campaign, fraud pattern
ends with a recommendation and a monitor (rolling rate with its interval, a guardrail line)
j.model: 1. Is it real? Which FPD (FPD30? FPD7?), which 'last month' (loans disbursed last month cannot have an FPD30 yet — so probably the month whose first due date passed 30 days ago), the same definition and payment cut-off as before, no pipeline change? Then the size: on Nur's app, the monthly vintages of January–July 2026 have 74–136 loans each with a readable FPD30 and 0–2 defaults each — June 1 of 136 (0.74 %), July 2 of 122 (1.64 %): that is 'FPD doubled', and it is one extra default; a 95 % interval on 2 of 122 runs from about 0.5 % to 5.8 %. If it is a handful, the answer is 'watch the next vintage and the three-month rolling rate', not an alarm. 2. If it is real, where is it? App version and device (a release can break the payment reminder or auto-debit), product term, grade and score band, region and the officer who reviewed it, acquisition source (a campaign or new partner), new vs repeat customers. Concentrated in one cell means a cause; everywhere means policy or the economy. 3. Mix or rate? Did the share of riskier applicants rise with the same rate inside each group, or did the rate rise inside groups? Compare the score distribution of approved applicants month on month. 4. Look for an event: a scorecard or cut-off change, a new pre-check, a payment-channel outage on the first due dates (FPD that cures), a campaign, a fraud pattern (same device, same phone prefix, first payment never made). 5. Recommend: if a cell is found, fix or stop it — pause the campaign, block the pattern, patch the release — and have collections call those loans in the first week; if it is mix, decide with risk whether the new segment pays (break-even FPD about 2.5 % on Micro). Either way, add FPD by app version to the weekly monitor with its interval. In two sentences: first I check it is not one or two defaults on a small vintage or a definition change; if it is real, I locate it, separate mix from rate, fix the cell or re-price the segment, and add a monitor.

w08d5-r1.q: **R1.** *What is the difference between DPD and FPD?* (A1)

rubric: DPD is a state of a loan today (days since the oldest unpaid due date), grouped in buckets
FPD is an event: the first instalment not paid within X days, and you say which X
says what each is used for (collections and PAR vs early warning and fraud) or gives a number
j.model: DPD (days past due) is a state of a loan today: as-of date minus the due date of the oldest unpaid instalment, 0 if nothing is overdue; grouped into buckets 0 / 1–30 / 31–60 / 61–90 / 90+. FPD (first payment default) is an event of a new loan: the first instalment was not paid within X days of its due date (X = 30 is common; some use 7 or 10 — always say which). DPD drives collections, PAR and provisions; FPD is the early warning for a new product, channel or scoring rule, and the main fraud signal, because it is known two months after disbursement. "On my project book FPD30 was 1.28 % — 1.70 % in the app against 1.04 % at branches — while PAR30 was 3.12 %; the two answer different questions."

w08d5-r2.q: **R2.** *PAR30 vs NPL — what is the difference?* (A2)

rubric: PAR30 = outstanding of loans with DPD > 30 ÷ total outstanding, on balance, not count
NPL is a classification: usually 90+, but it varies (60+, restructured, unlikely to pay)
warns against comparing ratios without checking the definition
j.model: PAR30 (portfolio at risk) = outstanding of loans with DPD > 30 ÷ total outstanding — a pure DPD measure, on balance, not on count. NPL (non-performing loans) is a classification: usually 90+ DPD, but depending on the regulator or the company it can be 60+, and it can include restructured or "unlikely to pay" loans regardless of DPD. NPL ratio = NPL outstanding ÷ total. On my project: PAR30 3.12 %, NPL90 2.55 % — so 2.55 of the 3.12 points were already old debt, not a fresh wave. The trap: comparing your NPL with a competitor's annual report without checking their definition.

w08d5-r3.q: **R3.** *What is a roll rate and how do you use it?* (A3)

rubric: the share moving from one bucket to the next between two month-ends (a migration matrix)
what it is used for: where collections effort pays, forecasting losses
a trap: the same DPD definition and cut-off in both snapshots, closed loans handled
j.model: The share of loans (or balance) in one delinquency bucket at one month-end that are in the next bucket at the next month-end — a migration matrix between two snapshots. It tells collections where effort pays and lets risk forecast losses: multiply today's buckets through the matrix to project next month. On my project, 1 September → 1 October: 19.5 % of 1–30 loans rolled to 31–60, 75.8 % cured; 31–60 → 61–90 69.6 %; 61–90 → 90+ 100 %. Reading: the first bucket is where contact matters — after 60 days almost nobody comes back. Traps: the snapshots must use the same DPD definition and the same payment cut-off; closed loans must be handled explicitly.

w08d5-r4.q: **R4.** *How do you compute approval rate? Why do two teams get different numbers?* (A5)

rubric: approved ÷ decided applications
names the denominator choices: cancelled, approved-not-disbursed, application vs decision month, pre-check rejects
ask for the definition, write it under the number, reconcile once
j.model: Approved ÷ decided applications is the usual risk convention; the differences are all in the denominator and the status list: are cancelled applications in it, is "approved but not disbursed" approved, is it counted by application month or decision month, per application or per customer, and does it include applications rejected by a pre-check before the customer submitted. On my project the app channel showed 68.2 % (approved ÷ decided), 58.2 % (approved ÷ app sessions) and 84.5 % (approved ÷ submitted forms) — three correct numbers. The answer: ask for the definition, write it under the number, reconcile once.

rubric: EL = PD × LGD × EAD, and what each part means
it is the mean loss, covered by pricing and provisions; the tail is covered by capital
says what is crude in a simple estimate
j.model: EL = PD × LGD × EAD, summed over loans: the probability of default (usually 90+ within 12 months or lifetime), the share lost if it defaults after recoveries, and the exposure at default. It is the mean of the loss distribution — the cost of doing business that pricing and provisions must cover; unexpected loss (the tail) is what capital covers. A crude version on my project (PD = share now 90+, LGD 60 % assumed) gave 3.60 bn, 1.77 % of the performing exposure, with grade C carrying 46 % of the loss on 27 % of the exposure. Then say what is crude: the PD mixes loan ages and understates long products; real banks estimate PD from vintages and scorecards and LGD from actual recoveries.

rubric: provisions cover the loss we expect, not only losses that happened
Stage 1: 12-month EL; Stage 2 (risk up significantly, ~30+ DPD): lifetime EL; Stage 3: defaulted (~90+)
why it matters: early delinquency costs money in the P&L now
j.model: Every loan carries a provision for the loss we expect, not only the loss that has happened. Healthy loans (Stage 1) carry 12 months of expected loss; loans whose risk has increased significantly — typically 30+ DPD or a large score deterioration — (Stage 2) carry lifetime expected loss; defaulted loans, typically 90+ (Stage 3), carry lifetime loss on a defaulted exposure. The PDs are forward-looking, weighted over economic scenarios. Consequence for an analyst: a rise in early delinquency moves loans to Stage 2 and costs money in the P&L now, before any loan is written off — which is why risk watches 1–30 entries and FPD so closely.

rubric: credit-loss charge of a period ÷ average portfolio, usually annualised
a flow in the P&L, while provisions are a stock on the balance sheet
puts it next to yield and funding cost, or names a company difference
j.model: The credit-loss charge of a period divided by the average portfolio, usually annualised: (change in provisions + write-offs − recoveries) ÷ average gross loans. It is a flow in the P&L; expected loss / provisions are the stock on the balance sheet. It sits next to the yield and the cost of funds in the metric tree: on my project the annualised yield was about 25.5 % against an assumed 18 % funding rate, so every point of cost of risk takes a large share of a 7.5-point spread. Company differences: gross vs net of recoveries, average vs opening portfolio.

w08d5-r8.q: **R8.** *Measure vs calculated column in Power BI?* (C3)

rubric: calculated column: per row, at refresh, stored — for slicing and filtering
measure: at query time, in the filter context — for anything aggregated
the classic mistake: a ratio as a column, then summed
j.model: A calculated column is computed once per row at refresh and stored — use it for attributes you slice or filter by (an age band, a DPD bucket, "is 90+"). A measure is computed at query time in the current filter context — use it for anything aggregated (outstanding, PAR30 %, collection rate): it gives the right answer at every level of a visual, the total included. The classic mistake is a ratio as a column, then summed — PAR30 of a region becomes the sum of loan-level percentages. On my project the six base measures (Outstanding 208 723 504 430, Disbursed Count 7 828, Avg Ticket 51 709 668, PAR30 3.12 %, …) matched the SQL views to the soum.

rubric: the probability of data at least this extreme, assuming the null hypothesis is true
says what it is not: not the chance the null is true, not the size of the effect
adds an effect size in business units
j.model: The probability, computed assuming the null hypothesis is true, of getting a result at least as extreme as the one observed. It is not the probability that the null is true, not "the probability it is due to chance", and not a measure of size. Example from my project: app vs branch FPD, 1.70 % vs 1.04 %, z = 2.15, p = 0.032 — if the channels truly had equal FPD, a gap this large would appear in about 3 % of samples of this size. Then the effect size: about 7 more first-payment defaults per 1 000 app loans.

w08d5-r10.q: **R10.** *What is a sample ratio mismatch and what do you do when you find one?* (D4)

rubric: the split between arms differs from the design more than chance allows (chi-square on counts)
it means assignment or logging is broken, so the result cannot be trusted
checks slices (device × week), removes the broken cell, reports it, never reweights
j.model: The split between arms differs from the design (e.g. 50/50 planned, 52/48 observed) by more than chance — a chi-square test on the counts. It means the assignment or the logging is broken and the arms may differ in who is in them, so the result cannot be trusted. Check it overall and by the slices the software ships in (device × release week): in my project the overall p was 0.09 ("fine") but iOS users in the last week went 60/40 (p ≈ 10⁻¹⁴) — a client bug; that cell was removed from both arms, reported, and the engineers fixed the client. Never "reweight" an SRM away.

w08d5-b5.q: **B5.** Your three questions for this interviewer — and, for one of them, why you are asking it.
w08d5-b5.h: B5. Your questions to the company (5 min)

rubric: two or three questions
about the work, the data or the team — not perks
at least one that follows from something said in the interview
you can say why you ask it
j.model: 1. "What would a successful first three months look like in this role?" 2. "You mentioned the board pack — which definition of NPL does it use, and does it match the regulator's?" — I ask because in my project two teams' approval rates differed by ten points only because of the denominator, and I would want to know the house definition from day one. 3. "What is the biggest data-quality problem the team lives with today?"

w08d5-plan.q: **C1.** Your own 30/60/90 for the job in your `job_ad.md` (HW 8.1): one concrete line per period — who you will meet, what you will own, which question you will answer.
w08d5-plan.h: A 30/60/90-day plan for your first analyst job

rubric: days 1–30: named internal clients and a glossary of their definitions, one report rebuilt and reconciled
days 31–60: one recurring report or dashboard owned end to end, one data-quality problem sized
days 61–90: one question nobody owns, delivered as a memo with an owner and a value
fits the job advert's actual requirements
j.model: For a risk-analyst role at a bank with an app and a branch network. Days 1–30: meet the head of risk, collections, the portfolio manager and the BI team; write a glossary of their definitions — DPD, FPD, NPL, approval rate — and where each differs from what I know; rebuild the monthly PAR30 and vintage pack and reconcile it to Finance's ledger to the soum. Days 31–60: own the weekly FPD monitor by channel and app version end to end, with intervals; find and size one data-quality problem (for example duplicate payments) and propose the fix to the data team. Days 61–90: answer a question nobody owns — say, the early-bucket strategy: who to contact first and what a third fewer roll-forwards would save — as a one-page memo with an owner and a value, and automate the manual part of the pack I inherited.

w09d1-sc.q: Two scatters: A has r = 0.95 and slope 10 000 soum per 1 m; B has r = 0.60 and slope 400 000 soum per 1 m. Which is the stronger straight-line relationship?
options: A — r measures how close the dots lie to a line
B — its slope is forty times larger
They are equal
You need R² to say
w09d1-sc.explain: Strength is r, steepness is the slope; they are different numbers (b = r · s_y / s_x) (→ section 1, 'Pearson's correlation r').

w09d1-sc.q: A line has r = −0.7. What share of the spread of y does it explain, in %?
w09d1-sc.explain: R² = r² = 0.49: the sign of r drops out of R² (→ section 1, 'R²').

w09d1-sc.q: The residuals of a line average exactly 0. What does that tell you?
options: The line fits well
Nothing about the fit — least-squares residuals always average 0 on the fitted rows; look at their shape and their averages by group
The model has no outliers
R² is 1
w09d1-sc.explain: The average is 0 by construction; patterns in the residual plot (fans, curves, groups) are what tell you about the fit (→ section 1, 'Residuals').

w09d1-l1.q: **Your turn.** At the same principal, which Auto loans pay the most each month?
w09d1-l1.h: The scatter plot — one dot per loan

options: The 24-month loans: the shorter the term, the bigger each payment
The 48-month loans: a longer loan costs more interest, so it pays more each month
All three terms pay the same at the same principal
You cannot tell from a scatter plot
j.explain: The same principal repaid over 24 months instead of 48 means bigger instalments: the 'o' fan sits on top. More interest in total does not mean a bigger monthly payment.

w09d1-l2.q: **Your turn.** What is r between `term_months` and `principal` on all 7 828 loans? Print it to 3 decimals.

j.starter: # r between the term and the principal, all loans
j.model:
print(round(loans["term_months"].corr(loans["principal"]), 3))
# 0.581 — moderate: longer loans tend to be bigger loans (Auto and SME are both long and big)

w09d1-l3.q: **Your turn.** Sales reads r = +0.335 and proposes longer terms "to raise the monthly payments". What do you tell them?

options: Lengthening a loan raises its payment — the book-wide r = +0.335 proves it
The +0.335 comes from mixing products: big products are also long ones; inside each product a longer term means a smaller payment
r = +0.335 is too weak to mean anything
Within-product correlations are wrong because the groups are smaller
j.explain: The product is the confounder. Hold it fixed and the sign flips: for the same product (and the same amount), more months means smaller instalments.

w09d1-l4.q: **Your turn.** Which sentence can you write in Nilufar's note?

options: Income and the requested amount are independent — proven
On 13 162 applications with an income, the amount does not rise or fall with income in a straight line; the scatter could still hide a curve, and income may still matter for repayment
Income should be dropped from every model
r is wrong because 838 applications have no income
j.explain: r = 0 rules out a straight-line link only. Say the row count, look at the scatter, and keep 'does it predict repayment?' as a separate question.

w09d1-l5.q: **Your turn.** Income (skewness 1.3) against the number of loans a customer has taken: which correlation do you report first?

options: Pearson — it uses the real values
Spearman — income is a skewed money column, and a few very high incomes should not decide the answer
Neither: correlation needs normal data
Both give the same number on any data
j.explain: Money columns are skewed; ranks stop a handful of very large values from steering the coefficient. Report Pearson next to it if the reader expects it.

w09d1-l6.q: **Your turn.** In the 3 × 3 matrix, which pair has the weakest straight-line link?

options: principal and monthly_payment (0.904)
principal and term_months (0.581)
term_months and monthly_payment (0.335)
Every pair is equally strong
j.explain: 0.335 is the smallest off-diagonal value — and the Simpson subsection showed it is a mix of products, not a real 'longer means bigger payment' effect.

w09d1-l7.q: **Your turn.** With a = −12.1 and b = 41.49 (thousand soum per 1 m), what monthly payment does the line give for a 300 m Auto loan, in thousand soum?

j.model: −12.1 + 41.49 × 300 = 12 434.9 ≈ 12 435 thousand soum, about 12.4 m soum a month.

w09d1-l9.q: **Your turn.** For Micro loans, r between principal and payment is 0.8156. What share of the spread of Micro payments does the principal explain, in %, to 1 decimal?

j.hint: With one x, R² = r².
j.model: 0.8156² = 0.665 → 66.5 %. The rest is mostly the term again: Micro loans run 3 or 6 months.

w09d1-l10.q: **Your turn.** In the residual plot of the Auto line, the three term groups spread further apart as the principal grows. What pattern is that?

options: A shapeless band around 0 — the line is fine
Residuals that fan out: small around small loans, large around large loans — the error grows with the amount
All residuals are positive
The residual plot is the same as the scatter plot
j.explain: A fan says the gap between the groups grows with x: a payment is principal × a term factor, so terms differ by a share of the amount, not by a fixed sum. A fixed shift per term will not fix it completely — the worked example shows what does.

w09d1-l11.q: **Your turn.** Which of these four Auto loans changes the slope most if you delete it?

options: The 50 m loan with a normal payment
The 400 m loan whose payment is 10 times too small
The 220 m loan whose payment is 10 times too small
A 220 m loan with a normal payment
j.explain: Influence needs both: far from the line (an outlier) and far from the average principal (leverage). The 220 m typo is an outlier with almost no leverage; the 400 m typo has both.

w09d1-l12.q: **Your turn.** With coefficients 6 581.94, 41.83 and −184.30, what monthly payment does the model give for a 200 m Auto loan over 48 months, in thousand soum?

j.model: 6 581.94 + 8 366 − 8 846.4 = 6 101.5 ≈ 6 102 thousand soum (6 102 with the unrounded coefficients too). The true annuity at 24 % over 48 months is 6.52 m — the straight-line model is about 0.4 m low here.

w09d1-l13.q: **Your turn.** A model of the payment on all five products: how many product dummies does it need?

options: 5 — one per product
4 — one product is the reference group
1 — a single column with the codes 1 to 5
2 — products and the intercept
j.explain: k groups → k − 1 dummies; the left-out product is the reference, and every dummy's coefficient is the gap to it. A single column of codes 1–5 would claim that SME (5) is 'five times' Micro (1).

w09d1-l14.q: **Your turn.** The Auto model (R² 0.961) is offered as a calculator for a 10 m loan over 6 months. What do you say?

options: Use it — R² is 0.961
Do not: 10 m and 6 months are outside the Auto data (50–400 m, 24–48 months); the model would say 5.9 m a month for a 10 m loan
Use it, but round the answer
Add 1.96 standard errors and use it
j.explain: 6 581.94 + 41.83 × 10 − 184.30 × 6 = 5 894 thousand soum a month for a 10 m loan — more than half the principal every month. The model never saw such a loan; R² inside the range does not carry outside it.

w09d1-p1.q: **P1.** *(scatter plot)* BNPL loans carry 0 % interest, so the payment is the principal divided by the term (3, 6 or 12 months). What does their scatter of payment against principal look like?

options: One round cloud
Three straight lines from 0, the steepest for 3 months (a third of the principal each month)
One straight line, because there is no interest
A U-shape
j.explain: payment = principal ÷ term: three lines through 0 with slopes 1/3, 1/6 and 1/12 (333, 167 and 83 thousand soum per 1 m). The scatter shows three exact rules; one line through all of them cannot.

w09d1-p2.q: **P2.** *(Pearson's r)* What is r between the principal and the payment for the 1 569 BNPL loans, to 3 decimals?

j.starter:
bnpl = loans[loans["product_id"] == 3]
# r between pm and pay_k, rounded to 3 decimals
j.model:
bnpl = loans[loans["product_id"] == 3]
print(round(bnpl["pm"].corr(bnpl["pay_k"]), 3))
# 0.662 — moderate, although every loan follows an exact rule: three lines mixed make one loose cloud

w09d1-p3.q: **P3.** *(correlation is not causation)* Loans with more collection calls go bad more often. A manager proposes fewer calls "to cut defaults". What is wrong?

options: Nothing — fewer calls, fewer defaults
The arrow runs the other way: late payment causes the calls; cutting calls would leave the late loans alone and probably raise losses
The correlation is too weak
Calls and defaults are independent
j.explain: Reverse causation: the calls are a response to arrears. A correlation never tells you which way the arrow points; the timeline and the process do.

w09d1-p4.q: **P4.** *(r = 0)* Join the loans to their customers' monthly income. On the loans with an income, what is r between income and principal, to 3 decimals? Print the row count too.

j.starter:
li = loans.merge(cust[["customer_id", "monthly_income"]], on="customer_id")
# keep the rows with an income, then print their count and r(income, principal) to 3 decimals
j.model:
li = loans.merge(cust[["customer_id", "monthly_income"]], on="customer_id")
li = li.dropna(subset=["monthly_income"])
print(len(li), round(li["monthly_income"].corr(li["principal"]), 3))
# 7362 0.004 — no straight-line link on 7 362 loans

w09d1-p5.q: **P5.** *(Spearman)* For the BNPL loans, Spearman's correlation between principal and payment, to 3 decimals?

j.starter:
bnpl = loans[loans["product_id"] == 3]
# Spearman between pm and pay_k, rounded to 3 decimals
j.model:
print(round(bnpl["pm"].corr(bnpl["pay_k"], method="spearman"), 3))
# 0.737, against Pearson's 0.662

w09d1-p6.q: **P6.** *(correlation matrix)* In a matrix of application columns you see r = 1.000 between `requested_amount` and the loan's `principal`. What do you do before building a model?

options: Use both — two strong predictors are better than one
Keep one: they are the same number twice (every loan was paid as requested), and together they make the coefficients meaningless
Drop both
Average them
j.explain: r = 1.000 means one column is a copy (or a rescaling) of the other. Two copies in one regression are perfect multicollinearity.

w09d1-p7.q: **P7.** *(the least-squares line)* Micro loans: r = 0.8156, the principal's standard deviation is 1.3228 m soum, the payment's 440.51 thousand soum. What is the slope, in thousand soum per 1 m, to 1 decimal?

j.hint: b = r × s_y / s_x.
j.model: 0.8156 × 440.51 / 1.3228 = 271.6 thousand soum per 1 m: every extra million soum of a Micro loan adds about 272 000 soum a month (Micro loans are short: 3 or 6 months).

w09d1-p8.q: **P8.** *(fitting it)* Fit the BNPL line with `np.polyfit`. Print the slope and the intercept to 1 decimal.

j.starter:
bnpl = loans[loans["product_id"] == 3]
# slope and intercept of pay_k on pm, to 1 decimal
j.model:
b, a = np.polyfit(bnpl["pm"], bnpl["pay_k"], 1)
print(round(b, 1), round(a, 1))
# 199.4 -11.2

w09d1-p9.q: **P9.** *(R²)* For BNPL, r = 0.662. What R², in %, to 1 decimal?

j.hint: R² = r² with one x.
j.model: 0.662² = 0.438 → 43.8 %. The term explains most of the rest.

w09d1-p10.q: **P10.** *(residuals)* Residuals of the BNPL line from P8: what is the average residual of the 3-month loans, in thousand soum, to 1 decimal?

j.starter:
bnpl = loans[loans["product_id"] == 3].copy()
b, a = np.polyfit(bnpl["pm"], bnpl["pay_k"], 1)
# residual = pay_k - (a + b * pm); then its mean by term_months
j.model:
bnpl["res"] = bnpl["pay_k"] - (a + b * bnpl["pm"])
print(bnpl.groupby("term_months")["res"].mean().round(1))
# 3: 583.5, 6: -120.6, 12: -477.7

w09d1-p11.q: **P11.** *(leverage)* Repeat the Auto typo (the largest loan's payment divided by 10). By how many % does the slope change, to 1 decimal?

j.starter:
x = auto["pm"]
y2 = auto["pay_k"].copy()
i = x.idxmax()
y2[i] = y2[i] / 10
# slope with the typo, slope without; print the change in %
j.model:
s1 = stats.linregress(x, y2).slope
s0 = stats.linregress(x, auto["pay_k"]).slope
print(round((s1 / s0 - 1) * 100, 1))
# -2.3

w09d1-p12.q: **P12.** *(several predictors)* For BNPL, fit payment ~ principal + term with `np.linalg.lstsq`. What is the term's coefficient, in thousand soum per month, to 1 decimal?

j.starter:
bnpl = loans[loans["product_id"] == 3]
# X = 1s, pm, term_months; then lstsq; print the coefficients rounded to 1 decimal
j.model:
X = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(bnpl)), bnpl["pm"], bnpl["term_months"]])
coef, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(X, bnpl["pay_k"], rcond=None)
print(coef.round(1))
# [ 757.   198.9 -109.9] — R² rises from 0.438 to 0.820

w09d1-p13.q: **P13.** *(a dummy)* Only the **6-month** Micro and BNPL loans: fit payment ~ principal + micro (micro = 1 for Micro). What is the micro coefficient, in thousand soum, to 1 decimal?

j.starter:
m6 = loans[loans["product_id"].isin([1, 3]) & (loans["term_months"] == 6)].copy()
m6["micro"] = (m6["product_id"] == 1).astype(int)
# X = 1s, pm, micro; lstsq; print the coefficients to 1 decimal
j.model:
X = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(m6)), m6["pm"], m6["micro"]])
coef, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(X, m6["pay_k"], rcond=None)
print(len(m6), coef.round(1))
# 1852 [-40.6 176.8  70.3]

w09d1-p14.q: **P14.** *(extrapolation)* The Micro line (slope 271.6, intercept 0.7, thousand soum per 1 m) is used to price a 50 m Consumer loan. What would it say, and should anyone use it?

options: 13.6 m a month — use it, R² is 0.665
13.6 m a month — do not use it: 50 m is ten times the largest Micro loan, and a 50 m Consumer loan really pays about 2.8 m (24 months) to 9.1 m (6 months)
0.7 m a month — the intercept
It cannot be computed
j.explain: 0.7 + 271.6 × 50 = 13 581 thousand soum. The Micro line encodes 3- and 6-month terms at 42 %; outside 0.5–5 m it is a guess, and here a bad one.

w09d1-hw1.q: **H1.** The Consumer line, payment (thousand soum) on principal (m soum): what is the slope, to 1 decimal?

j.hint: fit_line on the 2 418 Consumer loans (product_id 2), x = pm, y = pay_k.

w09d2-cc.h: 6. Company corner How a scorecard is built and kept

j.model: I fit a logistic regression of the log-odds of bad on the characteristics, usually binned and WoE-coded so each band has one weight. Then I pick the scale — for example 600 points at good:bad odds of 50:1 and 20 points to double the odds — so factor = PDO / ln 2 and offset = 600 − factor × ln 50, and each attribute's points come from its coefficient times its WoE times the factor; the applicant's score is the sum. j.hint: The swap-out set is m[m["credit_score"] < c], with c your C2 cut-off: its bads ÷ its loans.

w09d5-st.q: > 🚀 **Stretch (optional).** One cut-off for every product is the wrong question. Redo C2's contribution for **Consumer** loans (branch: acquisition 450 000, servicing 25 000 a month) and add it up by grade. Which grades lose money?
w09d5-st.h: What the mentor checks and what happens next

options: None — every grade pays
Only grade D
Grades C and D, as for Micro
Grades B, C and D
j.explain: Only grade D: 104 scored Consumer loans, 9.62 % bad, −10.8 m soum (−104 036 a loan). Grade C earns +310.3 m at 5.74 % bad, because Consumer's break-even PD is 7.79 % (Week 8 Day 2) against Micro's 4.23 %. So Consumer's line sits at 600, while Micro's thinner margin needs a stricter one (C2): the cut-off follows the product's margin, not the score alone. With EAD = the whole principal the answer is the same (D −42.9 m, C +174.9 m).
